hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric impetigo (ICD-10 L01.00) by secure video visit for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. For limited impetigo, TeleDirectMD uses topical mupirocin first-line and reserves oral antibiotics for extensive disease or suspected MRSA, consistent with Infectious Diseases Society of America skin-and-soft-tissue guidance, which keeps overall antibiotic exposure low. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

howItWorks.sectionTitle: How Online Pediatric Impetigo Treatment Works

steps.title: Confirm eligibility and book
steps.description: Verify the child is ages 5 to 17 and located in one of our 41 licensed states or Washington, DC, then book a video visit and complete the intake form. steps.title: Parent consent and ID verification
steps.description: A parent or legal guardian provides consent and verifies their identity at the start of the visit. The guardian must be present for the entire visit, which is required in every state for a minor's care.

steps.title: MD video evaluation
steps.description: A licensed physician (MD), never a nurse practitioner or physician assistant, evaluates the child by secure video, reviews history and any uploaded photos, and assesses lesion extent and MRSA risk to determine whether topical or oral therapy is appropriate.

steps.title: Treatment plan and prescription
steps.description: If appropriate, the physician sends a prescription to your pharmacy, choosing topical mupirocin for limited impetigo or an oral antibiotic for extensive or MRSA-suspected disease, and provides a written visit summary with school re-entry and follow-up guidance.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states require explicit consent documentation when oral antibiotics are prescribed by telehealth for pediatric skin infections. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

paragraphs: Impetigo is a common, contagious superficial bacterial skin infection caused mainly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep). It typically produces honey-colored crusted sores around the nose and mouth or on the limbs, and a bullous variant produces fluid-filled blisters.

Impetigo is most common in young children and spreads easily in schools and households, but limited cases respond well to topical antibiotics. Per CDC Group A Strep impetigo guidance, topical mupirocin is first-line for limited disease, and Infectious Diseases Society of America skin-and-soft-tissue guidelines reserve oral antibiotics for extensive or MRSA-suspected infection.

TeleDirectMD focuses on limited impetigo in children ages 5 to 17 that is well-suited for video assessment, with a parent present, and refers cellulitis, abscess, systemic illness, or post-streptococcal complications to in-person or emergency care.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric impetigo in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Staphylococcus aureus:
items.text: the most common cause, including some MRSA strains in certain communities.

items.label: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep):
items.text: another common cause, which can rarely lead to post-streptococcal kidney complications.

items.label: Breaks in the skin:
items.text: bacteria enter through cuts, insect bites, eczema, or scratched skin.

items.label: Warm humid weather and close contact:
items.text: schools and sports increase transmission risk.

items.label: Poor wound hygiene:
items.text: impetigo spreads by direct contact and shared towels, clothing, or bedding.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every crusted sore is impetigo. Cold sores (HSV), infected eczema, contact dermatitis, cellulitis, and ringworm can mimic it. TeleDirectMD uses photo review and clinical history to distinguish impetigo from look-alike conditions and directs deep, spreading, or systemic infections to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Impetigo vs Cold Sores (HSV)
compareCards.text: Impetigo produces honey-colored crusted sores that can occur anywhere but often appear around the nose and mouth and spread by contact. Cold sores from herpes simplex virus appear as grouped painful vesicles on the lips that recur in the same spot. The honey-colored crust and lack of recurrent grouped vesicles help distinguish impetigo from HSV.

compareCards.title: Impetigo vs Cellulitis
compareCards.text: Impetigo is a superficial infection with crusted surface lesions that respond to topical or short oral antibiotics. Cellulitis is a deeper infection with warm, tender, spreading redness, often with fever, and requires in-person evaluation and systemic antibiotics. Distinguishing depth and systemic features determines whether telehealth is appropriate.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If your child has deep, spreading, or systemic infection, an abscess, or signs of a post-streptococcal complication, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person or emergency care rather than treating by video.

treatmentOptions.intro: Limited impetigo, meaning a few lesions in one area, is treated with topical mupirocin. Extensive or bullous impetigo, or cases suggesting MRSA, may need an oral antibiotic such as cephalexin, clindamycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. sections.title: Limited impetigo

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Gently wash crusts with soap and water before applying the topical antibiotic.
Cover lesions and keep the child's nails short to reduce scratching and spread.
Wash hands often and do not share towels, clothing, or bedding until healed.
Most limited impetigo improves within a few days of starting mupirocin.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If lesions spread, multiply, or do not improve within 3 to 5 days, seek in-person care.
If fever or deep, warm, spreading redness develops, this may be cellulitis; seek in-person care.
If dark or reduced urine develops after impetigo, seek urgent care for a possible kidney complication.
Follow up by video if you are unsure whether the infection is healing as expected.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Keep cuts, bites, and eczema clean and covered to prevent new impetigo.
Children can usually return to school 24 hours after starting effective treatment and once lesions are covered.
Continue the full prescribed course even after lesions start to heal.
Replace or wash items that contacted the sores, such as towels and bedding.
Return for in-person care if lesions spread, fever develops, or there is no improvement in 3 to 5 days.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's impetigo online?
items.answer: Yes, for limited cases. TeleDirectMD treats impetigo (ICD-10 L01.00) by video for children ages 5 to 17 with a parent present. An MD examines the lesions and prescribes topical mupirocin for limited disease or an oral antibiotic for extensive or MRSA-suspected cases. The self-pay visit is $79, available in 41 states plus Washington, DC. Cellulitis or systemic illness requires in-person care.

items.question: What does impetigo look like, and how is it diagnosed over video?
items.answer: Impetigo produces red sores that rupture and form honey-colored crusts, typically around the nose and mouth or on the arms and legs. A TeleDirectMD physician diagnoses it by video for children ages 5 to 17 from this characteristic appearance and history. Bullous impetigo shows fluid-filled blisters. Lesions that are deep, warm, and spreading with fever suggest cellulitis and need in-person evaluation instead.

items.question: What antibiotics does TeleDirectMD prescribe for pediatric impetigo?
items.answer: For limited impetigo in children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD uses topical mupirocin 2% (Bactroban or Centany, labeled from 2 months) first-line. Extensive or bullous impetigo, or suspected MRSA, may need an oral antibiotic such as cephalexin, clindamycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, dosed by weight. This topical-first approach follows Infectious Diseases Society of America skin-and-soft-tissue guidance and keeps antibiotic exposure low.

items.question: Is impetigo contagious, and when can my child return to school?
items.answer: Yes, impetigo is contagious through direct contact and shared items. Per CDC, children ages 5 to 17 can usually return to school 24 hours after starting effective antibiotic treatment and once lesions are covered. TeleDirectMD counsels families to keep nails short, cover sores, wash hands often, and avoid sharing towels or bedding until the infection heals.

items.question: When does impetigo need oral antibiotics instead of a cream?
items.answer: Impetigo needs oral antibiotics when it is extensive, bullous, involves many lesions or a large area, or when MRSA is suspected. For these, TeleDirectMD physicians may prescribe weight-based cephalexin, clindamycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for children ages 5 to 17. Limited impetigo with only a few lesions is treated topically with mupirocin, consistent with Infectious Diseases Society of America guidance.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for an impetigo visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for impetigo. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: When should impetigo be seen in person instead of online?
items.answer: See in-person care if a child ages 5 to 17 has signs of cellulitis (deep, warm, spreading redness with fever), an abscess that may need drainage, widespread or recurrent MRSA disease, or dark or reduced urine after impetigo, which can signal a post-streptococcal kidney complication. TeleDirectMD treats limited impetigo online and refers these more serious presentations for in-person evaluation.

items.question: How much does an online impetigo visit cost for a child?
items.answer: An online pediatric impetigo visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, no insurance required, for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable, but is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.

items.question: How fast does impetigo improve with treatment?
items.answer: Most cases improve within 2 to 5 days. Limited impetigo usually improves within a few days of starting topical mupirocin, and lesions typically resolve within about a week of effective therapy. TeleDirectMD advises parents of children ages 5 to 17 to gently wash crusts before applying the cream and to return for in-person care if lesions spread, fever develops, or there is no improvement within 3 to 5 days.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat impetigo in children under 5?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats impetigo only for children ages 5 to 17. Although topical mupirocin is FDA-labeled from 2 months of age, TeleDirectMD's pediatric skin services begin at age 5. Younger children with impetigo should be evaluated by their pediatrician in person, particularly to confirm the diagnosis and rule out more extensive infection that may need oral antibiotics.

TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 for impetigo; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, and does not make new asthma diagnoses.
